rv.q: It's quite the searing couple of hours, and yet dispensed with poetic panache and, counterintuitive as it may seem, also a wry sense of humor.
While Marble may not satisfy everyone with its measured pacing and open-ended conclusion, The Gift Theatre delivers a compelling Chicago premiere of Marina Carr's thought-provoking play.
In the end, the play itself is like a marriage that goes off the rails.
I highly recommend Marble be on your list to see.
Carr’s play is excoriating and poetic but also often funny as hell.

With Martinovich's confident direction and the talents of four remarkable actors at its service, an uneven script is elevated into a gripping and ultimately devastating depiction of two marriages in free fall.
Marble is not a comfortable play but it's got a kind of heroic beauty: the heroism of showing up and loading the dishwasher.

But all the acting, directing and design skill in the world can’t save a play that starts strong and then goes off the rails, never managing to balance out its characters conflicting world views or find a closing cadence.
Excellent dialogue voiced by indubitably fine actors plus a polished crew makes this production a MUST SEE.
This staging of Marble effortlessly captures these feelings, and even more so, delightfully proves the malleability and persistence of this storied theater company.

cn.t: Marina Carr's darkly comic Irish drama earns praise for its powerful exploration of deteriorating marriages, elevated by Kay Martinovich's captivating direction and strong ensemble performances that bring wit and emotional depth to this Chicago premiere.
